claims.text: Uniform multi-element mixing in noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials produces a high degree of local lattice distortion.
High local lattice distortion stabilizes a single-phase nanostructure.
High local lattice distortion minimizes defects in the nanostructure.
A distortion-stabilized, single-phase structure yields a uniform distribution of catalytic active sites.
Uniformly distributed active sites govern reliable material formation and enhance catalytic performance.
Magnetron sputtering can produce nanostructured HEA material.
The proposed noble metal–based HEA particles have a random elemental distribution.
Changing deposition temperature and sputtering power can systematically increase local lattice distortion.
Conditions that increase elemental diffusion promote incipient phase segregation.
Local lattice distortion minimizes defect clustering and suppresses phase separation.
Suppressing phase separation ensures uniform dispersion of noble metal atoms at or near the catalyst surface.
High lattice distortion creates a rough energy landscape that equalizes the mobilities of surface atoms.
The distortion-created energy landscape inhibits phase segregation.
Irradiated refractory HEAs exhibit enhanced recombination effects that are mechanistically analogous to the proposed behavior.
Stable, uniformly distributed active sites lower activation barriers for reactant adsorption and conversion.
Relative to the baseline, the high-distortion sample will have more uniform particle morphologies and size distributions.
Relative to the baseline, the high-distortion sample will exhibit a higher catalytic turnover frequency and a lower apparent activation energy.

The proposed relationship is limited primarily to nanoscale, high-surface-area catalysts with well-controlled compositions and may fail in bulk or when other sintering or segregation mechanisms dominate.
